claim: Respiratory complex I reversibly couples NADH oxidation and ubiquinone reduction with proton translocation against transmembrane potential.
source: Respiratory complex I is a multi-subunit membrane protein complex that reversibly couples NADH oxidation and ubiquinone reduction with proton translocation against transmembrane potential.
evidence: This is a well-established functional description of complex I, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Complex I from Escherichia coli is among the best functionally characterized complexes.
source: Complex I from Escherichia coli is among the best functionally characterized complexes, but its structure remains unknown, hindering further studies to understand the enzyme coupling mechanism.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to extensive functional characterization in the literature, as indicated by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The structure of E. coli complex I was previously unknown.
source: Complex I from Escherichia coli is among the best functionally characterized complexes, but its structure remains unknown, hindering further studies to understand the enzyme coupling mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of prior complete structural data for E. coli complex I in the literature, as discussed in the introduction.

claim: The authors describe the single particle cryo-electron microscopy structure of the entire catalytically active E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs.
source: Here, we describe the single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the entire catalytically active E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The structure of E. coli complex I displays highly dynamic connection between the peripheral and membrane domains.
source: The structure of this mesophilic bacterial complex I displays highly dynamic connection between the peripheral and membrane domains.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data showing multiple conformations and relative movements between domains.

claim: The peripheral domain assembly is stabilized by unique terminal extensions and an insertion loop.
source: The peripheral domain assembly is stabilized by unique terminal extensions and an insertion loop.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing C-terminal extensions and the G-loop in the peripheral arm.

claim: The membrane domain structure reveals novel dynamic features.
source: The membrane domain structure reveals novel dynamic features.
evidence: This is supported by observations of conformational heterogeneity in MTMH8 and other structural features.

claim: Unusual conformation of the conserved interface between the peripheral and membrane domains suggests an uncoupled conformation of the complex.
source: Unusual conformation of the conserved interface between the peripheral and membrane domains suggests an uncoupled conformation of the complex.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing disrupted interfacial interactions and exposure of the Q-cavity to solvent.

claim: Complex I facilitates transfer of two electrons from NADH to ubiquinone coupled reversibly with translocation of four protons across the membrane.
source: It facilitates transfer of two electrons from NADH to ubiquinone, or its analogues, coupled reversibly with translocation of four protons across the membrane against trans-membrane potential (Galkin et al., 2006; Sazanov, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I function, supported by cited references.

claim: Structures of complete complex I from several eukaryotes, one thermophilic bacterium, and partial structure of the membrane domain of E. coli complex I have been determined.
source: Structures of the complete complex I from several eukaryotes (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Hunte et al., 2010; Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Zhu et al., 2016), one thermophilic bacterium (Baradaran et al., 2013), and the partial structure of the membrane domain of Escherichia coli complex I (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011), have been determined.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited structural studies.

claim: Mitochondrial complex I has a molecular weight of 1 MDa and comprises more than 35 subunits.
source: Mitochondrial complex I has a molecular weight 1 MDa and comprises more than 35 subunits (Wirth et al., 2016), whereas bacterial analogues are much smaller with molecular weight approximately 500 kDa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial complex I composition, supported by the cited reference.

claim: Bacterial complex I analogues have a molecular weight of approximately 500 kDa.
source: Mitochondrial complex I has a molecular weight 1 MDa and comprises more than 35 subunits (Wirth et al., 2016), whereas bacterial analogues are much smaller with molecular weight approximately 500 kDa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial complex I composition.

claim: Complex I from all characterized species contains homologues of 14 core subunits.
source: Complex I from all characterized species contains homologues of 14 core subunits; seven subunits each assemble into peripheral and membrane arms, joined at their tips and form the complex with a characteristic L-shape.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the conserved architecture of complex I.

claim: Seven subunits each assemble into peripheral and membrane arms of complex I.
source: Complex I from all characterized species contains homologues of 14 core subunits; seven subunits each assemble into peripheral and membrane arms, joined at their tips and form the complex with a characteristic L-shape.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I architecture.

claim: The peripheral and membrane arms are joined at their tips and form a characteristic L-shape.
source: Complex I from all characterized species contains homologues of 14 core subunits; seven subunits each assemble into peripheral and membrane arms, joined at their tips and form the complex with a characteristic L-shape.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I architecture.

claim: The peripheral arm contains binding sites for NADH, ubiquinone, and flavin mononucleotide (FMN).
source: The peripheral arm, exposed to the cytoplasm in bacteria or the mitochondrial matrix in eukaryotes, contains binding sites for NADH, ubiquinone, and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as well as eight or nine iron-sulfur clusters, seven of which connect the NADH and ubiquinone-binding sites (Sazanov, 2015) enabling rapid electron transfer (Verkhovskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the peripheral arm structure and function, supported by cited references.

claim: The peripheral arm contains eight or nine iron-sulfur clusters.
source: The peripheral arm, exposed to the cytoplasm in bacteria or the mitochondrial matrix in eukaryotes, contains binding sites for NADH, ubiquinone, and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as well as eight or nine iron-sulfur clusters, seven of which connect the NADH and ubiquinone-binding sites (Sazanov, 2015) enabling rapid electron transfer (Verkhovskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: Seven iron-sulfur clusters connect the NADH and ubiquinone-binding sites enabling rapid electron transfer.
source: The peripheral arm, exposed to the cytoplasm in bacteria or the mitochondrial matrix in eukaryotes, contains binding sites for NADH, ubiquinone, and flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as well as eight or nine iron-sulfur clusters, seven of which connect the NADH and ubiquinone-binding sites (Sazanov, 2015) enabling rapid electron transfer (Verkhovskaya et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN.
source: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN (E. coli nomenclature is used for the subunits hereafter) (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011), which are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters (Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the membrane arm structure, supported by cited references.

claim: The antiporter-like subunits NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters.
source: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN (E. coli nomenclature is used for the subunits hereafter) (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011), which are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters (Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Each antiporter-like subunit contains two structural repeats comprising five transmembrane helices (TMH4-8 and TMH9-13).
source: Each antiporter-like subunit contains two structural repeats comprising five transmembrane helices (TMH, TMH4-8, and TMH9-13).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of antiporter-like subunits, supported by prior structural studies.

claim: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane.
source: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane and the helix TM8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited structural studies.

claim: The helix TMH8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge.
source: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane and the helix TM8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited structural studies.

claim: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm.
source: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm and also contains five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits (Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: NuoH contains a five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits.
source: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm and also contains five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits (Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: NuoH together with subunits NuoB and NuoD forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity).
source: Together with subunits NuoB and NuoD it forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity) that stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the binding site of the ubiquinone head group (Q-site) found in the proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The Q-cavity stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the Q-site found in proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2.
source: Together with subunits NuoB and NuoD it forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity) that stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the binding site of the ubiquinone head group (Q-site) found in the proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane.
source: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane. These are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: The conserved ionizable residues in the membrane arm are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer.
source: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane. These are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited references.

claim: Rotation of the cytoplasmic half of TMH3 of NuoJ in mammalian complex I was associated with active-deactive transition.
source: Attempts to visualize conformational changes in the membrane domain (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Parey et al., 2018) have revealed rotation of the cytoplasmic half of TMH3 of NuoJ in mammalian complex I (Agip et al., 2018) and were associated with active-deactive transition.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited references.

claim: Proton translocation mechanisms without conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits were recently suggested.
source: Recently, proton translocation mechanisms without conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits were suggested (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited references proposing alternative mechanisms.

claim: All proposed coupling mechanisms remain largely speculative and require further validation.
source: However, all proposed coupling mechanisms remain largely speculative and require further validation by functional, biochemical, and structural methods.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: E. coli complex I has been studied using many biophysical and biochemical techniques.
source: It has been studied using many biophysical and biochemical techniques (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: E. coli complex I represents a highly attractive system to study the coupling mechanism due to the possibility of fast and extensive mutagenesis.
source: Combined with the possibility of fast and extensive mutagenesis (Pohl et al., 2007; Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), it represents a highly attractive system to study the coupling mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited capabilities of the E. coli system.

claim: E. coli complex I is fragile and dynamic in nature.
source: However, owing to its fragile and dynamic nature (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), high-resolution structures of this complex remain limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: High-resolution structures of E. coli complex I were previously limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain.
source: However, owing to its fragile and dynamic nature (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), high-resolution structures of this complex remain limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The peripheral arm structure was solved at 2.1 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present a single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs, with the peripheral arm structure solved at 2.1 Å resolution and that of the membrane domain at 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: The membrane domain structure was solved at 3.7 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present a single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs, with the peripheral arm structure solved at 2.1 Å resolution and that of the membrane domain at 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data.

claim: Twin-strep tag was added to genomically encoded subunit NuoF using a CRISPR-Cas9 based system.
source: Twin-strep tag was added to genomically encoded subunit NuoF using a CRISPR-Cas9 based system (Jiang et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the cited reference and figure.

claim: The tagging enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex.
source: This enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which was further reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The complex was reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2.
source: This enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which was further reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the experimental data.

claim: Mass photometry indicated that reconstituted complex I was homogeneous and monodisperse.
source: Mass photometry indicated that reconstituted complex I was homogeneous and monodisperse (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the mass photometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Reconstituted complex I was active in catalyzing NADH:ubiquinone-1 (Q1) and NADH:decylubiquinone (DQ) redox reactions.
source: Reconstituted complex I was active in catalyzing NADH:ubiquinone-1 (Q1) and NADH:decylubiquinone (DQ) redox reactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A.
source: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A but were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids (Sazanov et al., 2003) likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors in the absence or at low concentration of detergent.
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data.

claim: NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids, likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors.
source: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A but were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids (Sazanov et al., 2003) likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors in the absence or at low concentration of detergent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the activity data, comparing to cited reference.

claim: The lipid environment provided by the nanodisc is expected to mimic closely lipid vesicles in which reconstituted purified E. coli complex I was shown to pump protons.
source: While without compartmentalization the proton translocation activity cannot be assessed, the lipid environment provided by the nanodisc is expected to mimic closely lipid vesicles in which reconstituted purified E. coli complex I was shown to pump protons (Steimle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited reference showing proton pumping in vesicles.

claim: Multiple conformations of the complex that differed by relative positions of the peripheral and membrane arms were revealed by 3D classification.
source: Multiple conformations of the complex that differed by relative positions of the peripheral and membrane arms were revealed by 3D classification (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data processing results shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å.
source: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) resolving the interface between the arms; however, due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å.
source: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) resolving the interface between the arms; however, due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data explaining the resolution limitations.

claim: Focused refinement of each arm separately and subtraction of nanodisc density improved the resolution of peripheral and membrane arms to 2.7 Å and 3.9 Å, respectively.
source: Focused refinement of each arm separately and subtraction of nanodisc density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) improved the resolution of peripheral and membrane arms to 2.7 Å and 3.9 Å, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data processing results shown in the referenced figures and table.

claim: After density modification, the resolution of membrane arm improved to 3.7 Å.
source: After density modification (Terwilliger et al., 2020), the resolution of membrane arm improved to 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is supported by the data processing results using the cited method.

claim: Large fraction of the particles corresponds to the peripheral arm only, which may have dissociated during cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: Micrograph analysis, in contrast to mass photometry, revealed that large fraction of the particles corresponds to the peripheral arm only (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that may have dissociated during cryo-EM sample preparation.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data with an inference about the cause.

claim: Dissociated peripheral arm particles yielded 3D reconstruction to 2.8 Å resolution.
source: These yielded 3D reconstruction to 2.8 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), similar to the map of the peripheral arm of intact complex I.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction data.

claim: Joining two subsets and applying density modification improved resolution of the peripheral arm to 2.1 Å.
source: Joining two subsets and applying density modification improved resolution of the peripheral arm to 2.1 Å (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by the data processing results shown in the referenced table and figures.

claim: The final models include 4618 residues that account for 94.7% of the total polypeptide constituting the complex.
source: The final models include 4618 residues that account for 94.7% of the total polypeptide constituting the complex (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the model building results shown in the referenced table.

claim: The fold and arrangement of the E. coli complex I subunits is mainly similar to the structures of other complex I homologs.
source: The fold and arrangement of the E. coli complex I subunits is mainly similar to the structures of other complex I homologs.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other complex I structures.

claim: High RMSD values for structural alignments reflect long-range twisting and bending of arms observed between complex I from different species.
source: Somewhat high values of RMSD obtained for structural alignments of the entire complexes or its individual arms to Thermus thermophilus [RMSD 7.3 Å (4199 Cα) for entire complex, 4.3 Å (2070 Cα) for membrane arm, and 8.1 Å (2129 Cα) for peripheral arm] and ovine enzyme [8.5 Å (4007 Cα) for entire complex, 5.0 Å (1969 Cα) for membrane arm, and 8.4 Å (2038 Cα) for the peripheral arm] (Figure 1B) reflect long-range twisting and bending of arms observed between complex I from different species (Agip et al., 2018; Baradaran et al., 2013; Vinothkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural alignment data, supported by cited references.

claim: E. coli complex I conformations revealed two modes of relative arm rotation.
source: Comparison of E. coli complex I conformations reconstructed to better than 4 Å resolution revealed two modes of relative arm rotation (Figure 1C): (1) rotation around an axis that passes through the NuoH-NuoB interface and is tilted around 45 degrees out of the plane formed by the arms with an amplitude of at least 13 degrees, and (2) rotation around an axis parallel to the membrane and roughly perpendicular to the long axis of the membrane arm with an amplitude of approximately 4 degrees.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the different conformations resolved by cryo-EM.

claim: Relative arm movements in E. coli complex I have larger amplitudes and more diverse directionality than in mammalian and T. thermophilus complex I.
source: Although relative arm movements were observed in mammalian (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Zhu et al., 2016) and T. thermophilus complex I (Gutiérrez-Fernández et al., 2020), their amplitudes were smaller and movement directionality was less diverse.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited references showing differences in conformational dynamics.

claim: Despite significant relative arm movements, the structure of each arm was rigid and did not reveal different conformations apart from specific local dynamics.
source: Despite significant relative arm movements, the structure of each arm was rigid and did not reveal different conformations apart from the specific local dynamics discussed below.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claim: At 2.1 Å resolution, conformations of most side chains in the peripheral arm, positions of ions, and multiple water molecules were resolved unambiguously.
source: At an average resolution of 2.1 Å with the local resolution in the core reaching 2.0 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) conformations of most side chains in the peripheral arm, positions of ions, and multiple water molecules were resolved unambiguously (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution cryo-EM map.

claim: E. coli subunits NuoC and NuoD are joined in a single polypeptide, unlike other structurally characterized homologues.
source: Unlike other structurally characterized homologues, E. coli subunits NuoC and NuoD are joined in a single polypeptide.
evidence: This is a structural observation unique to E. coli complex I.

claim: The 35 amino acid-long linker between NuoC and NuoD includes an α-helix (residues 180–194) that interacts with subunit NuoB.
source: The 35 amino acid-long linker includes an α-helix (residues 180–194) that interacts with subunit NuoB (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The relative positions of all redox centers with FMN and nine iron-sulfur clusters, including off path cluster N7, are particularly well conserved.
source: The relative positions of all redox centers with FMN and nine iron-sulfur clusters, including off path cluster N7 (Sazanov and Hinchliffe, 2006), are particularly well conserved (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other complex I structures and the cited reference.

claim: E. coli peripheral arm has ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with lengths of 22–45 residues.
source: A distinctive feature of the E. coli peripheral arm is the presence of ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with a length of 22–45 residues and a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop (Figure 2A, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure and table.

claim: E. coli peripheral arm has a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop.
source: A distinctive feature of the E. coli peripheral arm is the presence of ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with a length of 22–45 residues and a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop (Figure 2A, Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure and table.

claim: These extensions are unique among structurally characterized complex I homologues and have a well-defined structure.
source: These extensions are unique among structurally characterized complex I homologues and have a well-defined structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison with other complex I structures.

claim: The extensions increase the interaction surface between the electron acceptor module and connecting module by a factor of three (from 1400 to 4600 Å2).
source: Similarly, the G-loop fills a crevice between NuoCD, NuoI, and NuoG subunits (Figure 2A) and together with the extensions increase the interaction surface between the electron acceptor module (NuoEFG) and connecting module (NuoICDB) by a factor of three (from 1400 to 4600 Å2), thus stabilizing the peripheral arm assembly.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the interface areas.

claim: The structural features (extensions and G-loop) are conserved within the Enterobacteriaceae family and are very common in the phylum Gammaproteobacteria.
source: These structural features are conserved within the Enterobacteriaceae family, are very common in the phylum Gammaproteobacteria and display high conservation of interfacial residues, particularly for the G-loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The extensions demonstrate a new evolutionary strategy for complex stabilization that was not observed in other complex I homologs.
source: They demonstrate a new evolutionary strategy for complex stabilization that was not observed in other complex I homologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and comparison with other homologs.

claim: A strong density near the NuoG surface coordinated by GAsp617, GGln632, GGlu647, GAsp731 and four water molecules was assigned to a Ca2+ ion.
source: A strong density near the NuoG surface coordinated by GAsp617, GGln632, GGlu647, GAsp731 and four water molecules (Figure 2B) was assigned to a Ca2+ ion.
evidence: This is based on the structural data and coordination geometry shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The coordination number, geometry, and ion-ligand distances of ca 2.5 Å support the assignment to Ca2+.
source: The coordination number, geometry, and ion-ligand distances of ca 2.5 Å (Zheng et al., 2008) as well as the 2 mM concentration of Ca2+ in the buffer support this assignment.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and the cited reference on coordination chemistry.

claim: Divalent ions are known to increase both the activity and stability of E. coli complex I.
source: Divalent ions are known to increase both the activity and stability of E. coli complex I (Sazanov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: GAsp731, one of the calcium ligands, is part of the G-loop, suggesting that Ca2+ stabilizes the fold of the G-loop and consequently, the peripheral arm.
source: One of the calcium ligands, GAsp731, is part of the G-loop, suggesting that Ca2+ stabilizes the fold of the G-loop and consequently, the peripheral arm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of Ca2+ coordination.

claim: The extensions spatially overlap with the supernumerary subunits of complex I from T. thermophilus and the structurally conserved supernumerary subunits of eukaryotic complex I.
source: The extensions spatially overlap with the supernumerary subunits of complex I from T. thermophilus (Sazanov and Hinchliffe, 2006) and the structurally conserved supernumerary subunits of eukaryotic complex I (Zhu et al., 2016; Table 3), consistent with the suggestion that the primary role of supernumerary subunits is to stabilize the complex (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and supports the cited hypothesis about supernumerary subunit function.

claim: 1170 water molecules associated with the peripheral arm were modeled at 2.1 Å resolution.
source: At 2.1 Å resolution, 1170 water molecules associated with the peripheral arm were modeled (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution structural data.

claim: The positions of 180 water molecules are conserved with those identified in the peripheral arm of ovine complex I.
source: The positions of 180 water molecules are conserved with those identified in the peripheral arm of ovine complex I (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Figure 2D, red spheres).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited structure.

claim: Most conserved waters are buried in the interior of the subunits, shielded from the solvent, and likely play a structural role in stabilizing the subunit fold.
source: Most of conserved waters are buried in the interior of the subunits, shielded from the solvent, and likely play a structural role in stabilizing the subunit fold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural positions of the water molecules.

claim: Only a few waters interact closely with iron-sulfur clusters and may influence their potential.
source: Only a few waters interact closely with iron-sulfur clusters and may influence their potential (Tables 4 and 5).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in the referenced tables.

claim: Water molecules close to or between iron-sulfur clusters are not more conserved than those in other parts of the complex, suggesting they were not evolutionary selected to optimize electron transfer rate.
source: The water molecules close to or between iron-sulfur clusters are not more conserved than those in the other parts of the complex, suggesting that they were not evolutionary selected to optimize the rate of electron transfer as was suggested (Schulte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on conservation analysis that contradicts a cited hypothesis.

claim: The FMN conformation and key water molecules in the NADH-binding pocket are conserved.
source: The FMN conformation and key water molecules in the NADH-binding pocket are conserved (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Schulte et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited structures.

claim: Water molecule W1060 is hydrogen bonded to the isoalloxazine ring N5 atom of FMN and to FGlu92, which likely acts as the activating group during catalysis of hydride transfer from NADH.
source: This includes W1060, hydrogen bonded to the isoalloxazine ring N5 atom of FMN and to FGlu92, which likely acts as the activating group during catalysis of hydride transfer from NADH (Fraaije et al., 2000; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural observation and the cited reference on catalytic mechanism.

claim: The structure does not support the involvement of FGlu93 carbonyl oxygen flipping in ROS regulation as previously suggested.
source: Schulte et.al. (Schulte et al., 2019) suggested a mechanism for regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by E. coli complex I that involves flipping the carbonyl oxygen of FGlu93 upon enzymatic reduction. Our structure unambiguously places the corresponding carbonyl oxygen in a conformation that points away from FMN (Figure 3A) similar to conformations found in the reduced and oxidized ovine complex I (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020), which does not support its involvement in ROS regulation.
evidence: This is based on structural observation that contradicts a cited hypothesis.

claim: E. coli-specific FHis400 replaces Leu residues found in other homologues and is in Van der Waals contact with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN.

evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison with other homologs.

claim: FHis400 imidazole ring interacts directly with the N3 cluster iron atom and forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of FCys357 coordinating N3.
source: E. coli-specific features in the FMN-binding pocket include FHis400 that replaces the Leu residues found in other homologues. FHis400 is in Van der Waals contact with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN; its imidazole ring interacts directly with the N3 cluster iron atom and forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of FCys357 coordinating N3 (Figure 3A).

claim: The tip of the 218–223 loop is flexible as in many complex I structures.

claim: In E. coli complex I, cluster N1a can be reduced by NADH due to its uniquely high potential (~ −0.3 V).
source: In E. coli complex I, cluster N1a can be reduced by NADH due to its uniquely high potential (~ −0.3 V), differentiating it from other characterized species in which N1a cannot be reduced by NADH (Birrell et al., 2013; Zu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Three specific differences in the chemical environment of N1a explain its higher potential in E. coli.
source: Comparison of the chemical environment of N1a with other high-resolution structures of complex I revealed three specific differences explaining the higher potential of the N1a cluster (Table 4): (1) E. coli-specific EAsn142 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97 coordinating the N1a cluster and with N1a S1 (Figure 3B), consistent with its mutation to Met decreasing potential by 53 mV (Birrell et al., 2013). (2) In E. coli, water molecule W74 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97. This water resides in a hydrophilic cavity created by E. coli specific EGly140, replacing the alanine residue found in other species. (3) Because of small differences in the backbone conformation of NuoF, the backbone nitrogen of FGly97 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys133 in E. coli and Aquifex aeolicus but not in Ovis aries (Figure 3B, Table 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and the cited reference on mutagenesis.

claim: E. coli-specific EAsn142 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97 coordinating the N1a cluster and with N1a S1, consistent with its mutation to Met decreasing potential by 53 mV.
source: Comparison of the chemical environment of N1a with other high-resolution structures of complex I revealed three specific differences explaining the higher potential of the N1a cluster (Table 4): (1) E. coli-specific EAsn142 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97 coordinating the N1a cluster and with N1a S1 (Figure 3B), consistent with its mutation to Met decreasing potential by 53 mV (Birrell et al., 2013).

claim: In E. coli, water molecule W74 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97, residing in a hydrophilic cavity created by E. coli specific EGly140.
source: (2) In E. coli, water molecule W74 forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of ECys97. This water resides in a hydrophilic cavity created by E. coli specific EGly140, replacing the alanine residue found in other species.

claim: The effect of proximal His residue on N3 potential is likely compensated by FTrp363 replacing the hydrogen bond donors found in other species.

source: However, the structure shows that the polar environment of N2 is very conserved (Figure 3C), including two water molecules, W211 and W438.

claim: Dimethylation of 49kDaArg85 prevents it from forming a hydrogen bond with BCys63, which should decrease N2 potential in the mitochondrial enzyme.
source: This modification prevents it from forming a hydrogen bond with BCys63, which should decrease N2 potential in the mitochondrial enzyme.

source: Therefore, computational modeling, now enabled by the high-resolution structure, will be required to explain the difference in the cluster potentials.

claim: The fold of subunit NuoH is similar to the structures of T. thermophilus and eukaryotic complexes with one important exception.

claim: HLys274, almost universally conserved in complex I and related hydrogenases, is found in the HTMH7 off the main pathways proposed for proton translocation.
source: Curiously, HLys274, almost universally conserved in complex I and related hydrogenases, is found in the HTMH7 off the main pathways proposed for proton translocation (Figure 4A), however, the length and flexibility of the side chain allow it to switch between the extracellular surface and center of the membrane.

source: This region is buried in the middle of NuoM and the density of surrounding helices is very well-resolved indicating local character of the disorder.

claim: In T. thermophilus, the cytoplasmic region of 13TM8 is rotated by two residues relative to E. coli structure.
source: Interestingly, in T. thermophilus the cytoplasmic region of 13TM8 is rotated by two residues relative to E. coli structure (Figure 4B) which results in repositioning of T. thermophilus 13Lys235 (MLys265 in E. coli) from the center of the second structural repeat (TM9-TM13) towards the interface between the structural repeats facing 13His218 (MHis248 in E. coli).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Higher mobility of the helical fragment at the interface of symmetry-related modules may indicate π-bulge-enabled helical rotation and its potential role in proton translocation.
source: Thus, higher mobility of the helical fragment situated at a critical position at the interface of symmetry-related modules may indicate π-bulge-enabled helical rotation and its potential role in proton translocation.

source: The interface between membrane and peripheral arms mediates the coupling of ubiquinone reduction to proton translocation across the membrane.

claim: The interface is highly conserved between complex I homologs and related membrane-bound hydrogenases.
source: It is highly conserved between complex I homologs and related membrane-bound hydrogenases (Baradaran et al., 2013; Grba and Hirst, 2020; Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and forms through interaction between subunits NuoB and NuoD of the peripheral arm with NuoH and the ATMH1-TMH2 loop of the membrane domain.

claim: Several interfacial regions of subunits NuoB, NuoD, and NuoI become more ordered upon complex formation.
source: Apart from several interfacial regions of subunits NuoB, NuoD, and NuoI that become more ordered upon complex formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Table 2), the membrane-facing surface of E. coli peripheral arm, including the residues lining the Q-cavity, is highly mobile in both dissociated and complexed arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: The membrane-facing surface of E. coli peripheral arm is highly mobile in both dissociated and complexed arms.
source: Apart from several interfacial regions of subunits NuoB, NuoD, and NuoI that become more ordered upon complex formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Table 2), the membrane-facing surface of E. coli peripheral arm, including the residues lining the Q-cavity, is highly mobile in both dissociated and complexed arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Rotation of the NuoB/NuoD module creates multiple openings in the interface between the arms large enough to allow water and proton exchange between the Q-cavity and bulk solvent.
source: Rotation of the NuoB/NuoD module creates multiple openings in the interface between the arms (Figure 5B). They are large enough to allow water and proton exchange between the Q-cavity and bulk solvent, suggesting that the ubiquinone bound within the Q-site can receive protons directly from the solvent.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The resolved conformations of complex I represent uncoupled states in which redox reaction is not coupled to proton translocation.
source: Therefore, we think the resolved conformations of complex I represent uncoupled states in which redox reaction is not coupled to proton translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations of the disrupted interface.

claim: The detergent-solubilized complex can catalyze redox reactions.
source: To better understand the reasons for the observed uncoupled conformation and the missing density for HTMH1, we purified E. coli complex I in detergent LMNG, showed that it can catalyze redox reactions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and solved its structure to resolution of 6.7 Å (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The structure of detergent-solubilized complex was solved to resolution of 6.7 Å.
source: To better understand the reasons for the observed uncoupled conformation and the missing density for HTMH1, we purified E. coli complex I in detergent LMNG, showed that it can catalyze redox reactions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and solved its structure to resolution of 6.7 Å (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The detergent-solubilized complex also displays high relative mobility of the arms and has uncoupled conformation.
source: The detergent-solubilized complex also displays high relative mobility of the arms (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and has uncoupled conformation (Figure 6).

source: Its peripheral arm is rotated even further away from the expected coupled state position than in the nanodisc-reconstituted structures.

This allows us to conclude that neither air-water interface nor reconstitution into nanodiscs cause the uncoupled conformations.

source: E. coli complex I is composed of the smallest number of subunits among all structurally characterized complex I homologs.

claim: The JTMH3 conformational states are either suppressed in the resting state of the bacterial complex or do not occur at all.

claim: MTMH8 displays localized disorder next to the π-bulge, indicating possible involvement of this helix in structural rearrangements associated with proton translocation.
source: Conversely, MTMH8 displays localized disorder next to the π-bulge, indicating possible involvement of this helix in the structural rearrangements associated with proton translocation, and to our knowledge, this represents the first indication of specific conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits.

source: Conversely, MTMH8 displays localized disorder next to the π-bulge, indicating possible involvement of this helix in the structural rearrangements associated with proton translocation, and to our knowledge, this represents the first indication of specific conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the observation.

source: Purified E. coli complex I is known to be more flexible and fragile than its homologs from other organisms (Morgan and Sazanov, 2008; Sazanov et al., 2003).
